item.title: Taming the Monster in Your Head
item.description:
The Inner Noise


Every dev knows the monster voice. The one that pops up at 2 PM with “you’re behind on tasks”, “that bug will never be fixed”, or worse — random replay of every embarrassing thing you’ve ever said on a standup call.

It’s not your code editor that’s noisy, it’s your mind.


Why It Gets Loud


Stress, deadlines, context switching — they all feed that inner chatter. And the more we try to “power through,” the louder it seems to get. No amount of caffeine or fancy gear will mute it.


Melting the Monster


Here’s what surprised me: when I started experimenting with ambient soundscapes, the voice lost its grip.

Not music, not lo-fi beats, but layered sounds that felt like they melted into the room.

Slowly, the fears, worries, and constant thought-looping quieted down.

It didn’t erase my problems, but it gave me the silence to actually think and code.


What About You?


Do you fight the inner noise with more stimulation, or have you found ways to turn it down?

If you’ve tried tricks that worked (or failed spectacularly), I’d love to hear them.

item.title: Hug a user is here! Tell us what’s broken, we’ll fix it
item.description:
We’re starting something new at daily.dev called Hug a User.


The idea is simple: Every week, each engineer gets up to half a day to fix a bug or ship a small feature that came directly from you. No tickets. No sprints. No begging for approvals (unless it’s the homepage, then yes, still sacred ground).



Basically, it’s your chance to have an engineer swoop in, cape and all, and make that one annoying thing disappear.


What counts?



  • Fixing a bug that’s been haunting you

  • Polishing rough edges that slow you down

  • Small features that would make your daily.dev experience smoother


What doesn’t count?



  • Asking us to build GitHub 2.0 in half a day

  • Secret plots to sneak your pet feature onto the homepage


So, tell us what’s the one bug, frustration, or small improvement you’d love to see us tackle in Hug a User?


Drop it in the comments, and who knows, next week you might log in and it’ll just be fixed.


(And yes, if you’ve ever cursed at daily.dev under your breath, now’s the time to turn that energy into a feature request.)

item.description: A guide to setting up a shared email domain for couples, allowing both partners to receive emails sent to either person's address at their custom domain. The setup involves purchasing a domain, connecting it to email accounts, and configuring forwarding rules. Benefits include keeping both partners informed on vendor communications, shared account management, and spam prevention through per-service email addresses. The author recommends choosing easily spelled domain names and provides specific setup instructions for Gmail and Fastmail.

item.title: Talking to an LLM
item.description:
My biggest cheat for 10x-ing the quality I get from ChatGPT? I talk to it. Literally.


There’s a simple rule in knowledge work: You can think more than you can say, and you can say more than you can type.


When it comes to working with LLMs, this matters a lot. Because the biggest unlock isn’t in the model… it’s in the context you give it.


Typing long, nuanced prompts is tedious. Most people start optimizing for brevity instead of clarity. But the thing is that LLMs thrive on context. The more details you give, the better the outcome.


That’s why I stopped typing, and started talking. Whether it’s ChatGPT, Claude, or Grok, I just speak my thoughts out loud. It feels weird at first (like talking to yourself), but it’s a real force multiplier.


If the tool you’re using has built-in voice transcription (like ChatGPT does), use it. If not, pair it with something like SuperWhisper. It works like magic.


This one shift has helped me 10x the quality of my work across product, marketing, operations, and sales. It’s my unfair advantage and I hereby offer it to you all for free :)


Highly recommend giving it a try.

item.title: We finally gave your posts what they deserve
item.description:
For the longest time, posting on daily.dev was a bit of a black box. You’d share something great, see a few upvotes roll in, maybe get a comment or two - and then what? Did people actually see it? Did it land? Did anyone care?
We didn’t give you much to work with. And that wasn’t good enough. Today, we’re changing that.


Introducing: post analytics


For the first time ever, you can now see how your posts perform - start to finish. Every impression, every upvote, every click to your profile, every Core you earned. It’s all in one place, with clean visuals and real insights.


You’ll finally understand:



  • How far your post traveled, and when it peaked.

  • Who engaged, and how it shaped your reputation.

  • What made people follow you, bookmark you, or even join your Squad.


This is your content command center:



  • Impressions, reach, and engagement - track your post’s life across time.

  • Reputation, Cores, and followers - know who you’re influencing and what you’re earning.

  • Boost data baked in (coming soon) - see when and how your post got amplified.

  • What works and what flops - adjust your strategy and become unignorably good.


We’re not talking vague stats. We’re talking actual signal. The kind that helps you get better, go bigger, or just brag when your post hits.



One more thing


If your post didn’t get the traction you hoped for, now you’ll know and can try something else instead.


If it did go viral? Now you have the receipts. Screenshots welcome.
Either way, your next great post starts here.


So go ahead. Open one of your posts. Watch the chart spike. Replay the moment it peaked.


You’re not just posting anymore. You’re publishing with purpose.

item.title: daisyUI 5 is here: What’s new and what to expect
item.description: daisyUI 5 represents a complete rewrite of the popular Tailwind CSS component library, offering significant performance improvements with 75% smaller bundle size and zero dependencies. The major changes include moving configuration from JavaScript to CSS files, introducing a powerful new theming engine with readable CSS variables and oklch color functions, and adding new components like Validator and List. The update also brings new style modifiers such as btn-soft and btn-dash, plus global effect variables for depth and noise. Migration involves updating package versions, moving plugin configuration to CSS, and updating some class names like card-compact to card-sm.

item.title: The end of notification hell
item.description:
Let’s be real - our old notification settings were… kinda lame. Patches on patches, broad toggles, zero finesse. We (finally) fixed that because our goal was simple: turn notifications into something actually useful, not just noise.


This is a complete makeover:



  • Ultimate control - Choose exactly what you get and where you get it: in-app, push, or email.

  • Granular as hell - Comments on your posts? Replies to your replies? Upvotes, mentions, Awards, cores, report updates? You decide!

  • Follow smarter - Fine-tune notifications for sources, users, collections, read later, streaks, achievements.

  • Creators rejoice - A whole section just for creator alerts so you never miss the metrics that matter.

  • Squads, finally fixed - One place for all your Squad notifications. And if you’re an admin or a mod, you now get pinpoint control for new members, posts awaiting review, milestones, and more.


Best part? You can split every single preference across in-app, push, and email. And you’ll find it all centralized in one screen. No hunting around. No more one-size-fits-none.


Building this wasn’t as simple as adding a few new toggles. Notifications touch almost every part of daily.dev - posts, comments, Squads, creators, achievements, moderation, email, push, in-app.


Untangling years of patch-on-patch logic and rebuilding it into one unified system was a massive refactor. It meant rethinking data flows, syncing across multiple channels, and making sure every edge case was covered so you don’t get spammed (or miss something important). It’s one of those projects that sounds small on the surface but is surprisingly hard to get right… which is exactly why we’re proud to finally ship it.


👉 Go and play with it yourself: app.daily.dev/settings/notifications


From now on, notifications aren’t spam. They’re a signal. And the signal is yours to control.
